opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the interest comes from a very natural place. When people started scaling up language models, there were these striking plots where, for some task, performance would sit near zero across a whole range of model sizes and then, at some scale, it would suddenly jump. That's exciting, because it suggests that just by making models bigger you might unlock qualitatively new capabilities you couldn't have predicted from smaller models. It's also a little scary, for the same reason. If abilities can appear sharply and unpredictably, then it's hard to know what the next, bigger model will be able to do, and that has real implications for safety, for planning, and for governance. So both the excitement and the concern come from the unpredictability.

What my collaborators and I, Rylan Schaeffer and Brando Miranda, wanted to understand was whether that sharpness is really a property of the models, or whether some of it comes from how we measure them. What we found is that a lot of these apparent emergent abilities show up when researchers use metrics that are nonlinear or discontinuous. Exact match is a good example. Say you're asking a model to do multi-digit arithmetic and you only give credit if every single digit is right. The model's per-token accuracy might be improving smoothly and predictably as you scale. But because you need everything right at once, that smooth improvement gets compounded, and the score looks flat at zero and then shoots up. If you instead use a continuous metric, like token edit distance or the probability the model assigns to the correct answer, then on the same model outputs the curve often looks smooth and quite predictable.

There are a couple of other factors as well. One is resolution. If you evaluate on a small test set, you just can't estimate small accuracies well, so everything below some threshold looks like zero. Another is how many model sizes you actually sample, since sparse sampling can make a gradual change look like a step.

I want to be careful about what we're claiming, though. We're not saying large models don't gain impressive new capabilities, and we're not saying emergence is impossible in principle. The claim is narrower. Many of the specific examples people pointed to can be explained by the researcher's choice of metric rather than a fundamental change in the model's behavior with scale. I think that's actually good news, because it means capabilities may be more predictable than they first appeared if we choose our measurements thoughtfully. It also shifts some of the responsibility onto us as evaluators. The way we design benchmarks and metrics shapes the story we tell about these models, so we should be deliberate about it, especially when those stories feed into policy and safety decisions.

r001.rationale: The response describes performance staying near zero across model sizes and then suddenly jumping as scale increases.

r002.rationale: It uses multi-digit arithmetic to illustrate metric effects, but does not say interest in arithmetic came from a hypothesis linking arithmetic ability to reasoning.

r003.rationale: It says the next larger model’s capabilities are hard to predict, but does not identify uncertainty about the scale at which abilities improve as the central concern.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's worth starting with what people actually mean when they say "emergent abilities." The way it's typically been framed is this idea that as you scale up models, there are certain capabilities that just aren't there, and aren't there, and aren't there, and then suddenly, at some scale, they appear. So the picture is a kind of phase transition, a sharp, discontinuous jump that you couldn't have predicted from looking at the smaller models.

And I think the reason that framing captured so much attention is that it has implications in two directions. On the excitement side, it suggests that if we just keep scaling, we might unlock new capabilities that we can't anticipate, and that's a very seductive story for anyone building these systems. On the concern side, the same unpredictability is exactly what makes people nervous. If you can't forecast what a model will be able to do until you've trained it, then it's very hard to do safety work ahead of time, very hard to plan, very hard to regulate. The whole idea that capabilities could show up unannounced is sort of the core of the worry.

So where our work came in was to ask a more basic question, which is: is that sharp, unpredictable jump a property of the model, or is it a property of how we're measuring the model? And what we found is that in a lot of the canonical cases, it's really the latter. When you look at these benchmarks, the metrics that produce the dramatic emergence curves tend to be discontinuous or nonlinear in a particular way. Exact match is a good example. If a model has to get every token of a multi-step arithmetic problem correct to get credit, then a model that's getting most of the tokens right scores zero, and a model that's slightly better scores one. The underlying improvement might be very smooth, the per-token accuracy might be rising gradually and predictably with scale, but the metric compresses all of that into a cliff.

And when you swap in a metric that gives partial credit, or you look at something like token edit distance, or you just increase the resolution of the evaluation by using more test examples so that your estimates at small scale aren't quantized to zero, the sharp jump largely goes away. You get a smooth, continuous, and importantly, predictable curve. We were also able to show the flip side of this, where we could take vision models, which nobody claims have emergent abilities, and induce emergence just by choosing a nonlinear metric. So the phenomenon is quite reproducible as a measurement artifact.

Now, I want to be careful about what we are and aren't saying. We're not saying that large models aren't more capable than small ones. They clearly are, and that's not in dispute. And we're not claiming there could never be a genuinely discontinuous capability. What we're saying is that the evidence that's been used to support the sharp-jump story is, in many cases, better explained by metric choice than by something fundamentally unpredictable happening inside the model. And that matters a lot for how you think about the concern, because if the underlying capability is actually improving smoothly, then it is, at least in principle, forecastable. You can study it in smaller models, you can extrapolate, and you can do the safety and planning work in advance.

So I guess my overall take is that the interest is understandable, and some of the concern is reasonable, but a lot of the specific anxiety about surprise is built on a measurement foundation that doesn't hold up as well as people assumed. And I think the more productive direction is to be much more deliberate about evaluation design, because the choices we make about what to measure and how are shaping the narrative about what these systems can do in ways that aren't always obvious.

r001.rationale: The response describes capabilities as absent at smaller scales and then seemingly appearing suddenly at some scale.

r002.rationale: Arithmetic is used to illustrate how exact-match metrics can create apparent emergence; the response does not link interest in arithmetic to a hypothesis about reasoning.

r003.rationale: The response presents surprise and difficulty forecasting capabilities as concerns, but does not identify uncertainty about the scale at which abilities improve as the central concern.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two questions that sometimes get mixed together. One is whether these models can do surprising things as we scale them up. Clearly, they can. The other is whether an ability really appears suddenly, or whether it looks sudden because of how we measure it.

Imagine evaluating a task where the model only gets credit if it produces the entire answer correctly. The model might be improving steadily, getting more pieces of the answer right, but your metric stays near zero until it can get all of them right together. Then you see a jump. If you instead measure partial progress, you might see a much smoother curve.

That distinction matters because a jump in a benchmark score isn’t necessarily evidence of a sudden change in the underlying capability. But it also doesn’t establish that every capability will be predictable. The concern is understandable: if a model can acquire abilities we didn’t anticipate, how do we evaluate it before deploying it? I think the productive response is to be more careful about our measurements and about what conclusions they support. Surprise is a reason to investigate, but it isn’t, by itself, an explanation.

r001.rationale: It describes models doing surprising things as they scale and explains how steady underlying improvement can appear as a jump in task performance under an all-or-nothing metric.

r002.rationale: It does not mention arithmetic ability or a hypothesis connecting arithmetic with reasoning.

r003.rationale: It discusses uncertainty about whether abilities appear suddenly and measurement effects, but does not identify uncertainty about the scale at which abilities improve as the central concern.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two questions that sometimes get mixed together. One is whether these models can do surprising things as we scale them up. Clearly, they can. The other is whether a capability actually appears suddenly, or whether our way of measuring it makes gradual improvement look sudden.

For example, suppose you score a task only when the model gets the entire answer exactly right. The model might be improving steadily, but that score stays near zero until it crosses some threshold. Then you see a jump and call it emergence. A measure that gives partial credit might show a much smoother curve.

That doesn’t make the capability less interesting, and it doesn’t mean every apparent emergence is a measurement artifact. But it does mean we should be careful about what the evidence supports. From a safety perspective, the concern is still important: we want to understand what a model can do before deployment. The useful question is how reliably we can measure and anticipate those capabilities, rather than whether we can attach the word “emergent” to them.

r001.rationale: It describes task scores appearing to jump as models scale up, while underlying improvement may be gradual.

r002.rationale: It does not mention arithmetic abilities or the hypothesis linking them to reasoning.

r003.rationale: It centers concern on measurement reliability and anticipating capabilities, not uncertainty about the scale at which abilities improve.
